e-3432.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
e-3432.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
e-3432.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

e-3433.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
e-3433.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
e-3433.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(2,-2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))j \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,i+\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-\frac{(-2)}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\,i+\frac{2}{8}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-2)}{‖∇f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{4}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(2,-2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))j \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,i+\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-\frac{(-2)}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\,i+\frac{2}{8}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-2)}{‖∇f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{4}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4)$, can be found by computing $∇f(5,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(5,4) & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}}j \\  & =\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(5,4)}{‖∇f(5,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\sqrt{{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}+{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\frac{\sqrt{41}}{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{41}(5i-4j)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2(\frac{3}{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(\frac{3}{2},1)}{‖∇f(\frac{3}{2},1)‖} & =\frac{-i}{1}=-i\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}

content.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
